textbookText: 141. The linear magnification of a mirror when the image is the same size as the object equals: A) 1 (unity magnification), occurring at the centre of curvature for a concave mirror B) 0 C) Infinity D) −1 always for any mirror

142. Which of these is TRUE about a plane mirror compared with curved mirrors (concept contrast)? A) A plane mirror can be thought of as a spherical mirror with infinite radius of curvature B) A plane mirror always magnifies the image C) A plane mirror forms real images only D) A plane mirror has a well-defined focal point like curved mirrors
143. In a concave mirror, if the object distance equals the focal length (u = f), the image is formed: A) At infinity B) At the pole C) At the centre of curvature D) Exactly at the focus itself

144. A ray incident on a spherical mirror through its pole obeys the law that: A) Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection with respect to the principal axis (acting as the normal at the pole) B) It always passes undeviated through the mirror C) It converges at the centre of curvature D) It is completely absorbed

145. Why can a convex mirror never form a real image of a real object (extraordinary geometric fact)? A) Because reflected rays from a convex mirror always diverge and only appear to meet behind the mirror B) Because convex mirrors absorb all incident light C) Because convex mirrors have no focal point at all D) Because convex mirrors only work with virtual objects
146. If the radius of curvature of a concave mirror is 20 cm, its focal length is: A) 10 cm B) 20 cm C) 40 cm D) 5 cm

147. An object 30 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm forms an image at (using 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, sign convention applied): A) 30 cm in front of the mirror (real image, at C, since u = 2f) B) 15 cm behind the mirror (virtual) C) At infinity D) 10 cm in front of the mirror

148. Spherical aberration in curved mirrors refers to: A) The failure of paraxial and marginal rays to converge at exactly the same focal point B) The formation of colored images due to dispersion C) The complete absence of any image D) The magnification being always greater than one

149. Why is a large concave mirror (rather than convex) preferred in reflecting telescopes to collect starlight (extraordinary application)? A) It converges the faint parallel rays from distant stars to a real, bright focal point for observation B) It diverges starlight to make the field of view wider C) It magnifies the image without needing any focusing D) It works only for nearby terrestrial objects, not stars
150. The relationship between magnification (m), image height (h′), and object height (h) is: A) m = h′/h = −v/u B) m = h/h′ only C) m = v + u D) m = h′ × h
